newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Infrastructure bond impact small - ITA.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Infrastructure bond impact small - ITA.

text.p: The Australian government's decision to abolish a tax break on infrastructure bonds should have no impact on existing projects and a limited one on new projects, the Infrastructure Trust of Australia (ITA) said.

Treasurer Peter Costello announced earlier this month that legislation would be introduced to prevent any more investors gaining access to the tax break, after an examination of the system which had been intended to promote private infrastructure investment found it was being exploited for tax minimisation.

"The effect of the abolition of infrastructure bonds is likely to be that the services provided by some projects may become more expensive for end-users, or that some projects may not go ahead because they are not economically viable," ITA associate director Ian Kay said in a statement.
"Some projects might also be delayed until such time as they do become economically viable, while some projects will be unaffected," he said.

Kay said ITA, Australia's only listed infrastructure fund, had assets which were financed using infrastructure bonds, but that no existing projects that have infrastructure bonds which had been certified would be affected by the new ruling.
The system had allowed developers to issue bonds whose interest attracted no tax.
Lenders could then offer a lower interest rate and although the developer could not claim the interest expense against income, the bottom line was a tax-break for the approved project.
"The introduction of the legislation will have no impact on projects in which ITA has invested," Kay said.
ITA's assets include interest in the Sydney M2 and M5 tollways, Melbourne's City Link and an agreement to purchase an interest in the Sydney Eastern Distributor.
ITA Group's board of directors includes two directors who are independent of the trust's sponsor, Macquarie Bank Ltd. Ian Kay is an associate director of Macquarie Bank.
